citation.claim: Teachers should explicitly teach pupils to plan, monitor and evaluate their learning. Planning includes understanding the goal, activating relevant prior knowledge, selecting strategies and allocating effort; monitoring includes self-testing and self-questioning and changing strategy; evaluating appraises the plan and its implementation.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (Quigley, Muijs and Stringer), Recommendation 2 and the plan–monitor–evaluate cycle.

eefCycle.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the PDF text of the summary of recommendations and Recommendation 2 (planning, monitoring, evaluating definitions). The guidance’s own worked examples are mostly secondary; primary adaptations here are proposals.

citation.claim: A sequence of activating prior knowledge, explicit strategy instruction, modelling, memorisation of the strategy, guided practice, independent practice and structured reflection can be applied across subjects, ages and content.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (Quigley, Muijs and Stringer), Recommendation 2, seven-step model.

eefSeven.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the seven-step model and its Year 9 fishbone example. The model is EEF guidance, not a tested primary routine.

citation.claim: Modelling by the teacher is a cornerstone of effective teaching; teachers should verbalise their metacognitive thinking, for example asking aloud what they know about problems like this and which ways of solving them they have used before.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (Quigley, Muijs and Stringer), Recommendation 3.

eefModel.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the summary bullet and Recommendation 3 text on verbalising metacognitive questions. No claim about effect size is taken from this section.

citation.claim: Challenge is needed to develop knowledge of tasks, strategies and oneself as a learner, but it must be at an appropriate level: pupils need the motivation to accept it, and tasks should not overload them, particularly when applying new strategies. Scaffolds such as worked examples reduce demands.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (Quigley, Muijs and Stringer), Recommendation 4.

eefChallenge.checked: 2026-11-18; Read Recommendation 4 (accepted challenge, motivation, cognitive overload, worked examples). The marshmallow-test discussion is not used.

citation.claim: Purposeful pupil–pupil and pupil–teacher talk, guided by the teacher, can build knowledge of cognitive and metacognitive strategies; the Year 4 example discusses what was tricky about making branching keys and then improves them.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (Quigley, Muijs and Stringer), Recommendation 5 and its Year 4 science example.

eefTalk.checked: 2026-11-18; Read Recommendation 5 and the Year 4 branching-key dialogue.

citation.claim: Children as young as three can engage in metacognitive and self-regulatory behaviours such as setting goals and checking understanding, but self-knowledge remains rather inaccurate until about eight years of age, with children over-optimistic about their knowledge.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (Quigley, Muijs and Stringer), Misconception 1.

eefYoung.checked: 2026-11-18; Read Misconception 1. The cited underlying studies were not separately fetched.

citation.claim: Metacognition is specific to the task and stronger with secure subject knowledge. There is little evidence for teaching metacognitive approaches in discrete learning-to-learn or thinking-skills sessions; pupils find it hard to transfer generic tips, although older learners can come to apply strategies more widely.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (Quigley, Muijs and Stringer), Misconceptions 2 and 4.

eefContext.checked: 2026-11-18; Read Misconceptions 2 and 4. Used to justify embedding strategies in subject tasks; not a claim that discrete sessions never help any pupil.

citation.claim: Pupils often make unrealistic judgements of learning and can feel, falsely, that cramming is working; explicit teaching about spaced practice, and tools such as post-test self-evaluation of errors and revision patterns, can improve the accuracy of their judgements.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (Quigley, Muijs and Stringer), Recommendation 6 (independent learning and judgements of learning).

eefJudge.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the Recommendation 6 passage on judgements of learning, cramming, spaced-practice instruction and post-test self-evaluation. The underlying experiment (reference 38) was not fetched.

citation.claim: Practice testing and distributed practice are rated high utility; elaborative interrogation, self-explanation and interleaved practice moderate utility; summarisation, highlighting, keyword mnemonics, imagery for text and rereading low utility.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-regulated Learning guidance report (Quigley, Muijs and Stringer), Table 1 (from Dunlosky et al. 2013).

eefTable.checked: 2026-11-18; Read Table 1 and its utility bands as reproduced from Dunlosky et al. (2013). The original PSPI article returned HTTP 403 and was not fetched directly.

citation.claim: Practice testing and distributed practice were rated the most effective strategies reviewed. Recall from memory is more beneficial than recognition, failed retrieval signals what needs restudying, and learners should keep testing themselves with feedback until each idea is recalled correctly, then return on another day.
citation.source: John Dunlosky, Strengthening the Student Toolbox: Study Strategies to Boost Learning, American Educator, Fall 2013 (practitioner summary of Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan and Willingham 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest), Practice Testing section.

dunTest.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the full American Educator article, Practice Testing section. College and middle-school examples are not age norms for primary learners.

citation.claim: Learners retain more when the same practice time is distributed rather than massed, yet many students believe massed practice is better because it feels more fluent at the time; younger students may need help setting up a study schedule.
citation.source: John Dunlosky, Strengthening the Student Toolbox: Study Strategies to Boost Learning, American Educator, Fall 2013 (practitioner summary of Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan and Willingham 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest), Distributed Practice section.

dunSpace.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the Distributed Practice section, including first-grade spelling and eighth-grade examples.

citation.claim: Elaborative interrogation asks why a stated fact is true and self-explanation relates new information to what is known or explains problem-solving steps. Learners must explain rather than paraphrase; younger students may need coaching to tell an explanation from a paraphrase, and elaborative interrogation is harder with little prior knowledge.
citation.source: John Dunlosky, Strengthening the Student Toolbox: Study Strategies to Boost Learning, American Educator, Fall 2013 (practitioner summary of Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan and Willingham 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest), Elaborative Interrogation and Self-Explanation section.

dunElab.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the Elaborative Interrogation and Self-Explanation section, including limits for younger students with little prior knowledge.

citation.claim: Interleaving different kinds of problems makes learners practise identifying which kind of problem they face; performance during practice can be lower than with blocked practice even when later test performance is better.
citation.source: John Dunlosky, Strengthening the Student Toolbox: Study Strategies to Boost Learning, American Educator, Fall 2013 (practitioner summary of Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan and Willingham 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest), Interleaved Practice section.

dunInter.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the Interleaved Practice section; its studies are mainly college-level, with a fourth-grade mention. Not used as a primary effect estimate.

citation.claim: Rereading and highlighting are popular with students but have shown limited or inconsistent benefits compared with more effective strategies.
citation.source: John Dunlosky, Strengthening the Student Toolbox: Study Strategies to Boost Learning, American Educator, Fall 2013 (practitioner summary of Dunlosky, Rawson, Marsh, Nathan and Willingham 2013, Psychological Science in the Public Interest), Rereading and Highlighting section.

dunLow.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the Rereading and Highlighting section. Survey percentages from an elite university are not used.

citation.claim: Principles include beginning a lesson with a short review of previous learning, presenting material in small steps, checking for understanding, providing models and scaffolds for difficult tasks, and weekly and monthly review.
citation.source: Barak Rosenshine, Principles of Instruction: Research-Based Strategies That All Teachers Should Know, American Educator, Spring 2012.

rosen.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the list of ten principles and the opening review section in the PDF. Not used as evidence for specific Learning to Learn routines.

citation.claim: Retrieval practice means bringing learned information to mind after some delay, for example by writing or sketching everything known about a topic, then checking notes to correct errors and see what is and is not known, and retrieving again later.
citation.source: The Learning Scientists, Learn How to Study Using… Retrieval Practice (student-facing post).

lsRetrieve.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the full student-facing post. It is a practitioner summary written by cognitive psychologists; it is not itself a study.

citation.claim: Spaced practice spreads the same study time over a longer period, needs advance planning, and should use effective strategies such as retrieval rather than rereading notes.
citation.source: The Learning Scientists, Learn How to Study Using… Spaced Practice (student-facing post).

lsSpace.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the full post. Its cramming-and-sleep remarks are not used.

citation.claim: Elaborative interrogation asks how and why questions about ideas, connects them to one another and to experience, compares how two ideas are similar and different, and checks the explanations against class materials.
citation.source: The Learning Scientists, Learn How to Study Using… Elaboration (student-facing post).

lsElab.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the main post (how/why questions, connections, similarities and differences, checking). Subject examples at the end are not reproduced.

citation.claim: In one university classroom study, quizzes written by students, which tended to be narrow and factual, did no better than baseline and student-written questions did worse; a strategy that works in research is not guaranteed to work in every implementation, so its effect should be checked.
citation.source: The Learning Scientists, Classroom Blunders: When Learning Science Goes Awry (an instructor’s account of a university classroom study).

lsBlunder.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the full post served at this URL (requested while looking for a learning-styles post; the citation describes the page actually served). It is a single university classroom account used only as a caution about implementation, not as evidence against retrieval practice.

citation.claim: The review found that studies claiming to support matching instruction to a learner’s supposed learning style (for example visual or auditory) almost all failed key criteria for scientific validity; it found no adequate evidence for the matching hypothesis.
citation.source: Association for Psychological Science, news release on Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork, Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence, Psychological Science in the Public Interest.

apsStyles.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the APS news release describing the Pashler et al. PSPI review. The PSPI article itself returned HTTP 403 and was not fetched; the claim is limited to what the release states.

citation.claim: Reading comprehension strategies include questioning to check comprehension, clarifying (identifying uncertain words or phrases and seeking information), summarising and activating prior knowledge; teachers model and scaffold them, then reduce prompting as pupils use them independently.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Improving Literacy in Key Stage 2, second edition, Recommendation 3.

eefLit.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the second-edition PDF text of the recommendations summary and the Recommendation 3 strategy definitions (prediction, questioning, clarifying, summarising, activating prior knowledge) and reciprocal reading description. KS2 context; adapted for ages 6–7 as a proposal.

citation.claim: Feedback should move learning forward by focusing on the task, subject or self-regulation strategies; comments about personal characteristics or vague remarks are less likely to be effective, praise may work better when specific, and pupils need planned opportunities to use feedback.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Teacher Feedback to Improve Pupil Learning guidance report, Recommendations 2 and 3.

eefFeedback.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the recommendations summary, Recommendation 2 (task, subject, self-regulation focus) and the grading/praise/effort discussion. Written-feedback policy sections are not used.

citation.claim: In this Year 6 randomised trial, pupils in schools receiving a growth-mindset intervention made no additional KS2 progress and showed no evidence of impact on measured self-efficacy, test anxiety or self-regulation, although they understood its messages; many comparison-school teachers were already familiar with growth-mindset ideas.
citation.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Changing Mindsets: Effectiveness trial evaluation report (Foliano, Rolfe, Buzzeo, Runge and Wilkinson, July 2019), key conclusions.

eefMindsets.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the key conclusions and security rating. Used only to avoid relying on mindset messages; not a claim that growth-mindset ideas are false.

citation.claim: Help seeking is treated as important for learning: self-regulated learners identify when they need help and where to seek it, adapt the help received and evaluate the result. Approaching others can be socially difficult and may explain help avoidance; one summarised sixth-grade study linked adaptive rather than avoidant help seeking with higher efficacy and achievement.
citation.source: Mäkitalo-Siegl and Fischer, Stretching the limits in help-seeking research, Learning and Instruction 21(2), 2011, guest editorial (author post-print).

helpSeek.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the author post-print of the guest editorial (aim and scope, summaries of the special-section studies). It summarises other studies, mainly with older learners; primary application is an adaptation.

citation.claim: Transfer, especially far transfer, very often does not occur, though sometimes it does. Low-road transfer is triggered by similar conditions; high-road transfer involves deliberate abstraction and a search for connections. Instruction can “hug” by practising approximations of the target performance and “bridge” by asking what general principles might apply elsewhere.
citation.source: D. N. Perkins and G. Salomon, Transfer of Learning, International Encyclopedia of Education, second edition, Pergamon, 1992 (copy hosted on CUNY OpenLab).

perkins.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the hosted chapter PDF (abstract, near/far transfer, low/high road, hugging and bridging). The host is a CUNY course site rather than the publisher.

citation.claim: A spotted pattern is not yet a justified rule: a sequence extended without explaining how it arises from the situation “might just break down”. Explaining structure, as in two different constructions of the matchstick squares that both give 3N + 1, justifies the generalisation.
citation.source: NRICH (University of Cambridge), Go Forth and Generalise.

nrichGen.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the full article (staircase/Fibonacci and matchstick 3N + 1 examples). Secondary-leaning examples; primary adaptations are proposals.

citation.claim: Treat responses as conjectures that may need modifying; teachers model questions such as what is the same and different, which example might refute a conjecture and which extreme example is worth testing, then fade this scaffolding so learners ask them.
citation.source: NRICH (University of Cambridge), Developing Mathematical Thinking: Conjecturing and Generalising.

nrichConj.checked: 2026-11-18; Read the guidance introduction and conjecturing-atmosphere section, including the quoted teacher prompts. Webinars and the Magic Vs task were not used.
